titre: France's First Social Law, and Its Non-Enforcement
accroche: 1841: France bans the employment of children under eight. Enforcement is entrusted to volunteer notables, neighbors of the industrialists.
contenu_vulgarise:
The French law of March 22, 1841 is generally presented as the country's first social law. It forbids employing a child under eight in manufactories, factories, and workshops. Between eight and twelve, the working day may not exceed eight hours; between twelve and sixteen, twelve hours. Night work, from nine in the evening to five in the morning, is forbidden to those under thirteen.

These figures already tell the state of affairs they are meant to correct, since a law was needed to make eight hours the maximum for a nine-year-old. They also carry a first limit, written into the text: the rules apply only to establishments with more than twenty employees. Small workshops, where a large share of children worked, stay entirely outside.

## Who Will Check

The decisive question, however, is not scope but enforcement. That is where the text comes apart.

Supervision is entrusted to unpaid commissions, appointed by the prefects and made up of local notables and volunteer entrepreneurs. Unpaid means without remuneration. Local means that these notables live in the same town as the industrialists they are meant to monitor, frequent the same circles, and belong to the same world.

The rest is easy to guess, and it is documented: these commissions perform their duties poorly, then in practice cease to function. The notables are reluctant to play inspector to industrialists of their own class. On days when an inspection is announced, the children are hidden or sent home for the day. Under the July Monarchy, the provisions of the law remain largely a dead letter. It will take several decades for a corps of state-paid inspectors to be established, and real enforcement dates from that point.

## What a Rule Without Machinery Does Not Do

The case is useful because it isolates one variable. The 1841 rule is clear, published, voted by a legitimate Parliament, and backed by penalties. It lacks only one thing: someone whose job it is to enforce it, and who has nothing to lose by doing so.

What fails here is the organ, not the norm. Volunteer oversight entrusted to those who share the interests of the people overseen is not weak oversight. It is null oversight, and predictably so. The difference between 1841 and actual enforcement owes nothing to any change in the text: it owes everything to the invention of a paid, independent administration endowed with the power to sanction.

That is why, in law, the question that matters is almost never “what is forbidden,” but “who has the power, the time, and the interest to check.”

repere.texte: The French law of March 22, 1841 entrusts its supervision to unpaid commissions of local notables and volunteer entrepreneurs, who perform their duties poorly and then cease to function: these notables are reluctant to inspect industrialists of their own class.

carte.punch: The question is almost never what is forbidden, but who has an interest in checking.
carte.idee: The French law of 1841 forbids employing children under eight in factories. Its enforcement is entrusted to volunteer notables from the same world as the industrialists they monitor. These commissions soon cease to function, and the law remains largely a dead letter.

quiz.question: Why did the 1841 French law on child labor remain largely unenforced?
choix: Its supervision was entrusted to volunteer notables from the same milieu as the industrialists being monitored
It carried no criminal penalty against employers in breach
It was suspended shortly after being passed because of the decade's economic crisis
Its text let prefects set it aside in industrial departments
quiz.explication: Enforcement fell to unpaid commissions of local notables and volunteer entrepreneurs. These notables were reluctant to inspect industrialists of their own class, and the commissions soon ceased to function. What was missing was the organ, not the rule.

quiz_supplementaire.question: From what number of employees did the 1841 law apply to establishments, leaving small workshops outside its scope?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the rules applied only to establishments with more than twenty employees, leaving out the small workshops where a large share of children worked.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what did some employers do on days when an inspection was announced?
choix: They temporarily raised the wages of the children they employed
They publicly posted the text of the law in the workshop
They hid the children or sent them home for the day
They called in a doctor to examine the children present
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that on days when an inspection was announced, the children were hidden or sent home for the day, which emptied the oversight of its purpose.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What maximum daily working time does the 1841 law set for children aged twelve to sixteen?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Between twelve and sixteen, the 1841 law sets the maximum day at twelve hours, against eight hours for children aged eight to twelve.
